A single living document maintained by members of the
[LENS Program](https://lens-program.github.io/lens-program/). It collects how identifiability,
recoverability, and related ideas are defined and used in different fields, side by side, so we
can see where fields agree, where the same word means different things, and what is still
unknown.

**Adding to it.** Use **Edit this page** (right margin) to edit this document directly on
GitHub. Add your field's definition *next to* the existing ones rather than rewriting them,
cite it (`[@key]`, with the entry added to `references.bib`), and add your name to the
section's contributors table. Mark proposed connections *(proposed)* and unresolved questions
*(open)*. Nothing here is a LENS consensus unless the text says the group agreed on it.

# Concepts {#concepts}

Each concept follows the same outline: core question, definitions across fields, formal
statement, examples, connections and distinctions, open questions, contributors. To add a
concept, copy the outline from any existing one.

## Identifiability {#identifiability}

### Core question

If we knew the distribution of the observable data exactly, with infinite data, could we pin
down the quantity of interest uniquely? Identifiability is a property of the **model and the
observation scheme**, not of a particular dataset or estimator.

### Definitions across fields

#### Parametric statistical models

> A model $\{P_\theta : \theta \in \Theta\}$ is identifiable if the map $\theta \mapsto P_\theta$
> is one-to-one: $\theta_1 \neq \theta_2 \Rightarrow P_{\theta_1} \neq P_{\theta_2}$.
> [@rothenberg1971identification; @paulino1994identifiability]

#### Econometrics

> The structural parameters of an economic model are identified if they can be recovered
> uniquely from the distribution of observables, classically from the reduced form.
> [@koopmans1949identification]

The word "identification" covers many distinct notions in econometrics: point, set, local,
generic, weak, and others. @lewbel2019identification surveys them.

#### Causal inference

> A causal estimand is identifiable, given a causal model (e.g. a DAG) and its assumptions, if
> it can be written as a unique functional of the observed-data distribution. Every model
> consistent with the assumptions and the observed distribution must give it the same value.
> [@pearl2009causality]

Here the object being identified is an **estimand**, not necessarily a model parameter.

#### Systems biology and dynamical systems

> A model is *structurally* identifiable if its parameters are uniquely determined by the
> model output under ideal conditions: noise-free, continuous observation of the measured
> outputs. [@bellman1970structural]

See [structural non-identifiability](#structural-non-identifiability) and
[practical identifiability](#practical-identifiability).

#### Bayesian inference

Identifiability is not required for a proper posterior. With a proper prior, a nonidentified
model still gives a well-defined posterior, and the data can update beliefs about nonidentified
parameters *through* their prior dependence on identified ones. If $\theta = (\theta_I,
\theta_N)$, where the likelihood depends only on $\theta_I$, then
$p(\theta_N \mid \theta_I, y) = p(\theta_N \mid \theta_I)$: the data never update the
*conditional* prior. [@poirier1998revising; @gustafson2015bayesian]

### Formal statement

Let $\mathcal{P} = \{P_\theta : \theta \in \Theta\}$.

- **Global identifiability:** $P_{\theta_1} = P_{\theta_2} \Rightarrow \theta_1 = \theta_2$ for
  all $\theta_1, \theta_2 \in \Theta$.
- **Local identifiability at $\theta_0$:** the same implication holds within some open
  neighbourhood of $\theta_0$. Under regularity conditions this is equivalent to a nonsingular
  information matrix at $\theta_0$. [@rothenberg1971identification]
- **Generic identifiability:** identifiability holds everywhere except on a measure-zero
  subset of $\Theta$. [@allman2009identifiability]
- **Identifiability of a functional $\psi(\theta)$:** $P_{\theta_1} = P_{\theta_2} \Rightarrow
  \psi(\theta_1) = \psi(\theta_2)$. A functional can be identified when $\theta$ is not.

### Examples

- $Y \sim N(a + b, 1)$: $(a, b)$ is not identifiable, but $a + b$ is.
- Finite mixtures are identifiable only up to relabelling of the components.
- Misclassified binary exposure: when sensitivity and specificity are unknown, prevalence is
  not identified from the error-prone measure alone. [@gustafson2005model]

### Connections and distinctions

- **[Structural vs. practical](#structural-non-identifiability):** a model can be identifiable
  in principle and still [practically non-identifiable](#practical-identifiability) with
  finite, noisy data.
- **[Partial identification](#partial-identification):** when point identification fails,
  the data may still restrict the quantity to a set.
- **[Recoverability](#recoverability):** *(proposed)* recoverability asks which
  functionals can be learned, and may hold when the full parameter is not identifiable.
- **Observability** (control theory): whether the system state can be reconstructed from
  outputs. It is the state analogue of parameter identifiability. *(needs a reference and an
  entry)*


### Open questions

- *(open)* Is there a common definition that covers parameters (statistics), estimands (causal
  inference), and states (control theory)? Or are these different questions?
- *(open)* How should "identified" be reported when it holds generically but fails at the
  parameter values that matter scientifically, e.g. at the boundary?

## Structural non-identifiability {#structural-non-identifiability}

### Core question

Does the model structure itself prevent the parameter from being determined, even with perfect,
noise-free, unlimited data? Collecting more of the same data cannot fix structural
non-identifiability. Only changing the model, the observations, or the information supplied
(constraints, priors, external data) can.

### Definitions across fields

#### Systems biology and dynamical systems

> A parameter is structurally non-identifiable when it cannot be determined uniquely even from
> ideal, noise-free model output. This typically happens because of a functional relationship
> among parameters (a manifold of parameter values that produce the same output).
> [@bellman1970structural; @raue2009structural]

In profile-likelihood terms, the profile likelihood of a structurally non-identifiable
parameter is **flat**. [@raue2009structural]

#### Statistical ecology (parameter redundancy)

> A model is parameter-redundant if it can be rewritten in terms of fewer parameters. A
> parameter-redundant model is not identifiable. [@catchpole1997detecting; @cole2020parameter]

Parameter redundancy is checked symbolically, through the rank of a derivative matrix of an
exhaustive summary of the model. This gives the number of estimable combinations, and which
ones they are.

#### Statistics

> The model $\{P_\theta\}$ fails to be identifiable: distinct $\theta$ give the same $P_\theta$.
> See [identifiability](#identifiability). [@rothenberg1971identification]

### Formal statement

There exist $\theta_1 \neq \theta_2$ with $P_{\theta_1} = P_{\theta_2}$. Typically the set
$\{\theta : P_\theta = P_{\theta_0}\}$ is a manifold of positive dimension. Its dimension is the
number of parameters minus the number of estimable combinations, i.e. the deficiency in
@catchpole1997detecting.

### Examples

- $Y \sim N(a + b, 1)$: only $a + b$ is estimable; the deficiency is 1.
- Grouped or normalised likelihoods: if a likelihood depends on predictors only through
  within-group shares (e.g. a multinomial allocation within each group), any term that is
  constant within a group cancels and is structurally non-identifiable. An external anchor that
  varies within groups is needed to identify it.
- Capture–recapture models where survival and capture probability for the final occasion
  appear only as a product. [@catchpole1997detecting]

### Connections and distinctions

- **vs. [practical identifiability](#practical-identifiability):** structural problems come
  from the model and persist with infinite data; practical problems come from limited, noisy
  data.
- **[Partial identification](#partial-identification):** the non-identified direction may
  still be bounded, giving an identified set rather than a point.
- **[Recoverability](#recoverability):** *(proposed)* the estimable combinations are
  exactly the functionals that remain recoverable.


### Open questions

- *(open)* Symbolic rank methods scale poorly. What is the right check for high-dimensional
  hierarchical or spatial models with thousands of latent effects?

## Practical identifiability {#practical-identifiability}

### Core question

The model may be identifiable in principle. But with the finite, noisy data we actually have,
can the parameter be estimated precisely enough to be useful? Practical non-identifiability is
a property of the **model together with the data**. More or better data can fix it.

### Definitions across fields

#### Systems biology and dynamical systems

> A structurally identifiable parameter is practically non-identifiable if its likelihood-based
> confidence interval extends to infinity in at least one direction, given the available data.
> [@raue2009structural; @wieland2021structural]

#### Econometrics (weak identification)

> A parameter is weakly identified when the data contain little information about it. In
> instrumental-variable and GMM settings, this happens when the instruments are only weakly
> related to the endogenous variables, and standard asymptotic approximations break down.
> [@stock2002survey]

#### Bayesian inference

There is no single definition. A common working notion: the posterior for the parameter is
dominated by the prior, so the prior and posterior overlap heavily. In latent class models,
@garrett2000latent use the prior–posterior overlap of each parameter as a diagnostic.

### Formal statement

*(no single formal definition)* Each field operationalises the idea differently:

- profile-likelihood interval unbounded at a chosen confidence level [@raue2009structural];
- weak-instrument asymptotics, where identification strength shrinks with sample size
  [@stock2002survey];
- prior–posterior overlap above a threshold [@garrett2000latent].

### Examples

- An ODE model where a rate constant can be estimated only if the system is sampled during a
  fast transient that the design misses.
- Hierarchical models with few groups: the between-group variance is identifiable but very
  poorly estimated.
- Instrumental-variable analysis with a weak first stage. [@stock2002survey]

### Connections and distinctions

- **vs. [structural non-identifiability](#structural-non-identifiability):** see that page.
  The profile likelihood is flat in the structural case, and finite but wide or one-sided in
  the practical case.
- **[Recoverability](#recoverability):** *(proposed)* practical identifiability is
  identifiability judged at the precision the data can deliver; recoverability asks the same
  question about functionals.


### Open questions

- *(open)* Is there a definition of practical identifiability that is not tied to a particular
  inferential framework (likelihood, GMM, Bayesian)?
- *(open)* How should practical identifiability be assessed for spatial and hierarchical models,
  where information differs by component and location?

## Partial identification {#partial-identification}

### Core question

Point identification fails. Can the observable distribution, together with credible
assumptions, still restrict the quantity to a set, and how small is that set?

### Definitions across fields

#### Econometrics

> A parameter is partially identified when the observable distribution, combined with the
> maintained assumptions, restricts it to a set (the *identified set*) that is larger than a
> point but smaller than the whole parameter space.
> [@manski2003partial; @tamer2010partial]

The emphasis is on weak, credible assumptions that yield bounds, rather than strong
assumptions that yield a point.

#### Bayesian inference

> In a partially identified model, the posterior does not concentrate on a point as $n \to
> \infty$. It converges to a limiting distribution over the identified set, and the shape of
> that distribution is set by the prior. [@gustafson2015bayesian]

@moon2012bayesian show that Bayesian credible sets and frequentist confidence sets for the
identified set can disagree even asymptotically.

### Formal statement

Given the observed-data distribution $P_0$ and model $\{P_\theta\}$, the identified set is
$\Theta_I = \{\theta \in \Theta : P_\theta = P_0\}$. For a functional, it is $\Psi_I =
\{\psi(\theta) : \theta \in \Theta_I\}$. Point identification is the special case where
$\Psi_I$ is a single point.

### Examples

- Bounds on a mean with missing outcomes and no assumption about the missingness mechanism
  (worst-case bounds). [@manski2003partial]
- Misclassification with sensitivity and specificity known only to lie in ranges.
  [@gustafson2005model]

### Connections and distinctions

- **[Identifiability](#identifiability):** point identification is the degenerate case.
- **[Structural non-identifiability](#structural-non-identifiability):** structural
  non-identifiability produces an identified set; partial identification studies its size and
  shape.
- **[Recoverability](#recoverability):** *(proposed)* a functional that is constant over
  $\Theta_I$ is fully recoverable even when $\theta$ is only partially identified.


### Open questions

- *(open)* How should we report uncertainty when part of it can be reduced with more data and
  part of it never can?

## Recoverability {#recoverability}

### Core question

Given the data and the model we have, which target quantities can be learned (recovered), even
when the model as a whole is not identifiable?

### Definitions across fields

#### Missing data (graphical models)

> A target quantity (e.g. a joint distribution or a causal effect) is recoverable if it can be
> computed consistently from the distribution of the observed, partially missing data, given
> the assumptions encoded in a missingness graph (m-graph). [@mohan2013graphical]

#### Causal inference: selection bias and data fusion

> A query is recoverable from selection-biased data if it can be computed from the distribution
> of the selected sample, possibly together with external unbiased data, under the assumptions
> in the causal graph. [@bareinboim2014recovering; @bareinboim2016causal]

#### Inverse problems and compressed sensing

> "Recovery" of a signal refers to reconstructing it exactly or stably from incomplete
> measurements under structural conditions such as sparsity.
> [@candes2006robust]

#### LENS working usage

> *(interpretation, not settled)* Recoverability asks which **functionals** of a
> non-identifiable or partially identified model can be learned. These may be identified
> functionals, functionals with informative bounds, or functionals whose posterior
> concentrates even though the full parameter's does not.

### Formal statement

*(no single formal definition; candidates below)*

- **Identified functional:** $\psi$ is recoverable if $P_{\theta_1} = P_{\theta_2} \Rightarrow
  \psi(\theta_1) = \psi(\theta_2)$. See [identifiability](#identifiability).
- **Graphical recoverability:** $Q$ is recoverable if $Q(M_1) = Q(M_2)$ for every pair of models
  $M_1, M_2$ compatible with the graph that agree on the observed-data distribution.
  [@mohan2013graphical]
- **Bayesian learning** *(proposed)*: the posterior for $\psi$ differs from its prior, or
  concentrates, as $n \to \infty$. [@gustafson2015bayesian]

### Examples

- $Y \sim N(a + b, 1)$: $a + b$ is recoverable, $a$ is not.
- Recovering a population distribution from a selected sample when selection depends only on
  variables that are measured. [@bareinboim2014recovering]
- Exact recovery of a sparse signal from far fewer Fourier coefficients than the signal length.
  [@candes2006robust]

### Connections and distinctions

- **vs. [identifiability](#identifiability):** in causal inference and missing-data work,
  "recoverable" and "identifiable" are close to synonyms; the difference is mainly the setting
  (missingness or selection). *(proposed; needs discussion)*
- **[Partial identification](#partial-identification):** a functional constant over the
  identified set is recoverable. Others are recoverable only up to bounds.
- **[Practical identifiability](#practical-identifiability):** a recoverable functional can
  still be estimated imprecisely.


### Open questions

- *(open)* Should LENS adopt one definition of recoverability, or keep several labelled
  definitions (graphical, Bayesian, bound-based)?
- *(open)* How can recoverability be diagnosed in practice for complex hierarchical, spatial,
  or measurement-error models?

# Connections across fields {#connections}

This section maps how the [concepts](#concepts) relate, and where different fields use
different words for similar ideas. Rows marked *(proposed)* are interpretations awaiting
discussion, not settled correspondences.

## How the concepts relate

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  ID["Identifiability<br/>(point)"]
  SNI["Structural<br/>non-identifiability"]
  PI["Partial<br/>identification"]
  PRI["Practical<br/>identifiability"]
  REC["Recoverability<br/>(of functionals)"]
  SNI -- "failure of" --> ID
  SNI -- "yields an identified set" --> PI
  ID -- "with finite, noisy data" --> PRI
  PI -- "functionals constant on the set" --> REC
  ID -- "of a functional" --> REC
```

## Rough equivalences between fields

| Idea | Statistics | Econometrics | Causal inference / missing data | Systems biology | Ecology |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Model determines the target uniquely | identifiability | (point) identification | identification; recoverability | structural identifiability | — |
| Model cannot determine it, even with infinite data | non-identifiability | under-identification | non-identifiable estimand | structural non-identifiability | parameter redundancy |
| Data carry little information about it | weak information *(proposed)* | weak identification | — | practical non-identifiability | near-redundancy |
| Target restricted to a set | — | partial / set identification | bounds | — | — |
| Some functions still learnable | identified functionals / estimable functions | — | recoverable queries | identifiable combinations | estimable combinations |

Empty cells are invitations: if your field has a term, add it.

## Same word, different meaning

- **"Identification"** in causal inference concerns an *estimand* given a causal model. In
  parametric statistics it concerns *parameters* given a probability model.
  [@pearl2009causality; @rothenberg1971identification]
- **"Recovery"** in compressed sensing is about reconstructing a signal under sparsity. In
  missing-data work it is about computing a quantity from the observed-data distribution.
  [@candes2006robust; @mohan2013graphical]
- **"Structural"** means "intrinsic to the model equations" in systems biology, but "the causal
  or economic model behind the reduced form" in econometrics.
  [@bellman1970structural; @koopmans1949identification]

# Open questions {#open-questions-all}

Questions LENS cannot yet answer, collected from talks, the concepts above, and discussion. Each
item records who raised it and where. When a question is resolved, or turns into a project,
note it here rather than deleting it.

## From the LENS charter

These are the questions on the [LENS Program page](https://lens-program.github.io/lens-program/).

1. What are the relationships among identifiability, partial identifiability, practical
   identifiability, and recoverability?
2. Which parameters or functionals remain recoverable when a full model is nonidentifiable?
3. How can recoverability be characterized or diagnosed?
4. How do priors, constraints, measurement error, and external information affect what can be
   learned?
5. How do spatial and hierarchical structures influence identifiability?
6. How do likelihood-based and objective-function approaches relate?
7. How should we represent uncertainty when information varies across model components?

## Raised in the concepts above

- Is there one definition that covers parameters, estimands, and states?
  ([Identifiability](#identifiability))
- Checking structural identifiability for high-dimensional hierarchical and spatial models.
  ([Structural non-identifiability](#structural-non-identifiability))
- A definition of practical identifiability that does not depend on the inferential framework.
  ([Practical identifiability](#practical-identifiability))
- Reporting uncertainty that is part reducible, part irreducible.
  ([Partial identification](#partial-identification))
- One definition of recoverability, or several labelled ones?
  ([Recoverability](#recoverability))
